q: Explain the mechanism by which screwcap-sealed wine ages differently from cork.
accept: oxygen transmission rate lower reductive slower development tin liner
ans: Lower and more consistent oxygen transmission (especially tin-lined) slows tertiary development and raises reduction risk — while removing cork-borne TCA and sharply narrowing bottle variation (winery-sourced TCA and liner-to-liner OTR spread remain)
exp: Not better or worse: a different maturation curve, chosen deliberately.

q: Explain how climate change alters cellaring assumptions for classic regions.
accept: riper lower acid higher ph earlier peaks uncertain curves
ans: Riper fruit, higher alcohol and pH, lower acid — drinking windows may open earlier and the historic thirty-year curves can no longer be assumed
exp: An honest Master answer says: we do not yet know, and that is the point.

q: Explain how you would build a cellar for a restaurant opening in twelve months.
accept: buy back vintages now allocations mature stock storage cashflow phasing
ans: Secure allocations and mature back-vintages early while cash allows, phase deliveries against storage and cashflow, and open with depth in the categories the kitchen demands
exp: The list you open with was bought a year before anyone tasted the food.

q: Explain the 'dumb phase' in a maturing wine, and how you manage a cellar and a wine list around it.
accept: a closed phase between primary and tertiary character managed by tasting in depth
age ingrat when the wine shuts down so buy multiples and check bottles
the dumb period between youth and maturity keep it off the list and warn guests
the wine goes mute in transition so taste on a schedule and do not judge on one bottle
ans: A closed period — the French âge ingrat, the awkward age — in which a wine that showed beautifully young simply shuts down: fruit recedes, the nose goes mute, structure stands exposed without flesh around it, and the bottle tastes worse than it did at release and worse than it will again. It is best understood as the handover from primary aromatics to tertiary ones, alongside polymerising phenolics and slow ester hydrolysis. Timing is grape-, vintage- and producer-specific: classed-growth Bordeaux and Barolo classically go quiet somewhere from a few years after release into their second decade. Management is procedural. Buy in depth so you can spend bottles on information rather than guessing. Taste a case bottle on a schedule and write down what you find. Keep closed wines off the by-the-glass list and out of pairings you cannot rescue. Warn the guest before opening one, or steer them toward a wine that is drinking now. And never condemn a wine on a single closed bottle — the mistake that empties cellars of wines that were about to arrive.
exp: Drinking windows get discussed as if maturation were a smooth curve. It is not — it dips, and the dip is where reputations for 'disappointing' vintages are made. The Master-level content here is the management protocol, not the phenomenon.

q: A guest asks whether to buy fine wine as an investment. Give the honest case for and the case against.
accept: finite supply and low correlation against costs illiquidity and fraud risk
returns at the blue-chip end but storage fees premiums and thin liquidity
argue scarcity and track record then costs counterfeits and concentration risk
the case is scarcity the case against is cost illiquidity and fraud
ans: For: at the blue-chip end the market has delivered equity-like returns with relatively low correlation to equities; supply is genuinely finite and shrinks as bottles are drunk; and the market is now transparent enough to price and liquid enough to exit for a narrow band of famous labels, with Liv-ex providing the benchmark. Against: it pays no yield while you hold it; storage, insurance and in-bond fees compound year after year; the round trip is expensive once a seller's commission and a twenty to twenty-five per cent buyer's premium are both counted; liquidity is thin outside a hundred or so names; provenance risk and outright counterfeit sit on the downside; and the index is concentrated enough that Bordeaux and Burgundy sentiment moves everything. Tax treatment varies by jurisdiction and is a question for an accountant, not a sommelier. Then say the last part plainly: I am not a financial adviser, this is not advice, and the only guaranteed return on a bottle of wine is drinking it.
exp: The examiner is testing two things at once: whether you know the market's cost structure, and whether you know where a sommelier's authority stops. Explain the mechanics fully, decline to advise, and hand the tax and portfolio questions to the professionals who carry the licence for them.

q: Beyond visual authentication, what technology now protects a bottle — and what does it still fail to stop?
accept: bubble tags nfc chips taggants and loggers but old vintages and refills remain
tamper-evident seals and databases cannot protect pre-existing bottles or stop refilling
authentication tech verifies packaging not liquid and old wines predate it
prooftag nfc and dna markers with the refill and legacy-vintage loopholes
ans: Producers ship tamper-evident capsules and seals; unique bubble-tag or holographic labels whose random pattern cannot be duplicated; laser-etched or moulded marks in the glass; invisible DNA or chemical taggants in ink, capsule or glass; NFC and QR chips that authenticate against the estate's database and break on opening; and temperature-and-shock loggers travelling with the case. Several estates now run bottle-level registries, and append-only ledgers are used to record the ownership chain. What none of it stops: everything that predates it — the entire pre-2000 fine-wine universe is unprotected, which is exactly where the counterfeiter works, because nobody fakes current-release wine that can be verified. Nor does it stop the refilling of a genuine, verifiably authentic bottle, or the transfer of a real capsule onto a fake; a chip authenticates the packaging, never the liquid. And a ledger is only as honest as its first entry: a blockchain records a lie faithfully forever. Technology raises the cost of forgery and pushes it backwards in time; provenance chain, estate records and a sceptical palate still close the case.
exp: The whole counterfeit market lives in the gap this question describes. Every anti-counterfeit measure protects the bottles least likely to be faked, so the trade's real defences remain unglamorous: an unbroken paper trail, direct ex-cellar purchase, and a willingness to say no to a bargain.

q: On paper Alsace's appellation count leapt from three to fifty-three in 2011, with not one new row of vines delimited. What happened?
opts: Bas-Rhin and Haut-Rhin were each given a regional appellation of their own
Vendanges Tardives and Selection de Grains Nobles were raised from label terms to appellations
Every grand cru site became a separate appellation, replacing the single shared Alsace Grand Cru
Cremant d'Alsace was split into separate white and rose appellations
exp: Each of the fifty-one grand cru sites received a cahier des charges of its own in 2011, replacing the single shared Alsace Grand Cru appellation of 1975, while regional Alsace and Cremant d'Alsace carried on unchanged. The vineyards did not move an inch; the point was legal machinery, since a site with its own decree can tighten yields, admit a grape or sanction a blend without dragging fifty others through the amendment.

q: Red wine reached the top of Alsace's hierarchy for the first time with the 2022 vintage, at two grand crus long planted to Pinot Noir; a decree of July 2024 admitted a third. Which three?
opts: Hengst, Kirchberg de Barr and Vorbourg
exp: Hengst and Kirchberg de Barr had built serious Pinot Noir reputations across decades in which the grand cru tier admitted only white wine, and their amended decrees let the red carry the site name from the 2022 vintage; Vorbourg joined them when the arrete of 4 July 2024 rewrote its cahier. Each keeps its white rules too, so a Hengst may still be a Gewurztraminer; the red is an addition, not a replacement.

q: A 2005 amendment let one Alsace grand cru, Zotzenberg, write a grape from outside the noble four into its rules, honouring what its growers had always done best. Which grape?
exp: Sylvaner had grown on Zotzenberg's marl and limestone for generations while the noble-grape rule kept its name off the label, and the 2005 amendment recognised the tradition rather than inventing one. The concession is strictly local: on no other cru may the word Sylvaner appear, and Zotzenberg keeps the noble four alongside it.

q: Site, vintage and the words Alsace Grand Cru appear on a bottle of Altenberg de Bergheim, yet nowhere does it name a grape. What does that silence say about what is in the bottle?
accept: it is a blend of varieties
exp: Altenberg de Bergheim and Kaefferkopf are the crus whose rules sanction a blend, and a blended grand cru names no variety at all: the site is the whole claim. A single-variety bottling from the same slope still carries its grape, so the absent line is information, not an oversight.

q: Between plain Alsace and the crus, bottles labelled Alsace Cote de Rouffach or Alsace Ottrott occupy a rung of their own. What are those added names?
opts: Bereich names kept from the German decades for export labels
Communal denominations added to the appellation rules in 2011
Fantasy names registered by merchant houses and protected as trademarks
Grand cru sites relegated for exceeding their permitted yields
exp: The 2011 rules wrote a family of geographic denominations into AOC Alsace, communal names such as Cote de Rouffach, Vallee Noble and Ottrott among them, giving the region the middle ground it lacked between anonymous regional wine and the crus. Several are tied to Pinot Noir rather than to whites: Ottrott, Rodern and Saint-Hippolyte earned their names on the red.

q: Below the grand cru tier an Alsace grower may still put a vineyard name on the label, and the rules charge for the privilege. What do they demand of the wine?
accept: lower yields and higher minimum ripeness
lower yields and higher must weights
a smaller crop and riper grapes
a lower yield and a higher minimum ripeness
ans: Lower yields and higher minimum ripeness than plain Alsace
exp: A lieu-dit bottling must come in under a lower yield ceiling and reach a higher minimum ripeness than plain Alsace, the same bargain the crus strike at a higher pitch. The reward is a specific slope on the label without waiting for a grand cru list that has not grown since 2007.

q: Picking for Vendanges Tardives, a Riesling grower in Alsace needs the must to reach a legal minimum sugar concentration. Give the figure.
exp: Riesling and Muscat qualify for Vendanges Tardives at 235 grams of natural sugar per litre of must, while Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris, which fatten far more easily, face 257; the figures were raised to those levels in 2001. Chaptalisation is banned outright for the term, so every gram must hang on the vine into the autumn.

q: Shrivelled Gewurztraminer coming in for Selection de Grains Nobles faces the stiffest sugar minimum in the Alsace rulebook. What is the figure?
exp: Gewurztraminer and Pinot Gris must reach 306 grams of sugar per litre of must for Selection de Grains Nobles, against 276 for Riesling and Muscat. At that concentration ferments crawl and stop early of their own accord, which is why an SGN is always frankly sweet where a Vendanges Tardives merely promises ripeness.

q: A parcel of clean, late-picked Alsace Pinot Gris comes in at 260 grams of sugar per litre of must. Which of the region's two late-harvest terms is within reach?
exp: The Vendanges Tardives floor for Pinot Gris stands at 257 grams per litre, so 260 clears it with a little in hand. Selection de Grains Nobles sits far above such fruit for the same grape and expects shrivelled, nobly rotted berries besides, so clean bunches at this ripeness leave one word open and one out of reach.

q: Since the 2021 vintage a dryness indication is compulsory on Alsace's still whites, either as a printed scale or as one of four words. Which four?
exp: The four words track the European bands: sec up to roughly four grams of residual sugar with some latitude where acidity is high, demi-sec to about twelve, moelleux to about forty-five, doux beyond. A producer who prefers not to print words may use the graduated dryness gauge instead, but one or the other must appear.
